name: Yara Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do nights on the trunking runs for a parcel network, which means I drive an articulated truck from one big sorting hub to another, down the motorway and back. I start at nine in the evening, hook up a trailer full of parcels, drive three hours, swap trailers, and drive home. I like the quiet and the podcasts. What wears me out is the coupling, getting the trailer hooked on first time in the dark, because I've only been on artics eight months and I'm still clumsy at it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use an AI assistant on my phone for loads of things, planning my rest stops, checking a weird warning light, even writing the newsletter for our union branch. I share a house with two friends and I've got about nine months of money saved, plus a bit in an index fund from when I was living at home. My mate Kofi on the same run calls me the gadget girl.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, actually, because I like the tools. But I'd post that this is a good moment for the union to push on pay and rest breaks, since nobody can threaten us with robots anymore. Kofi would be unbearable about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. Motorway trunking is the first job everyone said robots would take, and if that doesn't happen, I've got a well-paid job for years. My only worries are getting better at coupling and the toll nights take on your sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the runs and keep using the AI stuff for the little things. I'd put more into the index fund, maybe two hundred a month. And I'd run for branch secretary, because someone young needs to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a tiny bit of boredom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tools save time. Where, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the assistant found me a rest area with showers that was open at three in the morning, which saved me forty minutes of driving around. It also helped me write a letter to the depot about the broken lights in the trailer park. Small stuff, but it adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you push for as branch secretary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper rest areas that women feel safe in, for a start. Then a night allowance that keeps up with prices. If the robots aren't coming, then the fight is the old one, about pay and conditions.

say: I'd say I'm a bit **disappointed**, because I like the **tools**.
I'd say it's time for the union to push on **pay and breaks**.
think: Motorway **trunking** stays a **well-paid job** for years in this picture.
My worries are **coupling** in the dark and the toll nights take on **sleep**.
do: Keep using **AI tools** for rest stops and letters.
Put about **two hundred** a month into the index fund.
Run for **branch secretary** of the union.
S0.quote: If the robots aren't coming, then the fight is the old one, about pay and conditions.
fieldNote: She's the rare driver who'd be **disappointed** the AI didn't arrive.
She sees the plateau as a chance for **old-style union** gains.
Her concern for **safe rest areas** for women came up unprompted.

steps.text: Keep doing the night trunking runs between the parcel hubs
Add about two hundred a month to her index fund
Stand for union branch secretary this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one is about the people in offices, not us, at least at first. Online I'd be sharing union stuff about making sure workers get a share of the savings, not just shareholders. I'd say it calmly, because panic helps nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is a target sooner than people realise. Hub-to-hub on the motorway is the easiest driving there is to automate, with no shoppers and no tight streets. So even if robots spread slowly, my bit of trucking might be the first one they try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking at the control room jobs at the hub, the people who watch the trucks on screens and plan the trailers. I'd do one of those short online logistics courses this year, the ones that cost a couple of hundred. And I'd use the union newsletter to warn everyone that night trunking is first in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Curious, but uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the control room. Isn't that the thinking work AI takes first here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's the catch, I spotted it while I was saying it. The planning bit goes to software, but someone still has to watch the screens and sort out a truck that's stuck. I'd try to be the person who knows both the cab and the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Kofi take your warning in the newsletter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh and say I've been reading too much on my phone. He's forty-two, with kids, and he's been on this run for nine years. I worry about him more than me, because I can move and he can't really.

say: I'd say this picture hits **office workers** first, not drivers.
I'd push for workers to get a **share of the savings**.
think: **Hub-to-hub** motorway driving is the **easiest to automate**.
My part of trucking might be the **first** they try, even if robots are slow.
do: Look into **control room** jobs at the hub.
Take a **short online logistics course** this year for about two hundred.
Warn members in the **union newsletter** that night trunking is first.
S1.quote: Hub-to-hub on the motorway is the easiest driving there is to automate, with no shoppers and no tight streets.
fieldNote: She **knows exactly** why her run is the most exposed kind of driving.
She caught her own **contradiction** about the control room in real time.
Her **worry for a colleague** with kids runs stronger than for herself.

steps.text: Take a short online logistics course for about two hundred
Apply for a control room role at the parcel hub
Write a union newsletter piece warning that trunking goes first
Use AI tools to learn the hub's trailer-planning system

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that the gains from this belong to everyone, because it's built on all our work and data. I'd be campaigning for some kind of shared income or public ownership of the robot fleets. At the hub I'd be getting people to sign up to the union in their dozens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my run goes first, around 2031, maybe sooner for motorway trucks. The control room jobs I wanted go in 2028, because that's thinking work. So I'd be thirty-one with no driving and no office job to step into, and I'd need something else completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look hard at which hands-on trades last longest, and I'd probably start training as a wind turbine technician or something with heights and weather. I'd keep the savings and the index fund as they are. I'd also use the AI tools to learn faster, because if AI is going to beat me, it may as well teach me first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, which feels wrong to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the two-year warning matter so much for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because three years after 2028 is 2031, and that's no time to finish a trade properly. With two years' warning, I'd have to start retraining almost straight away, while still doing nights to pay for it. I'd be shattered, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said excited. What part excites you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If all of that is real, the world gets rebuilt from scratch, and I'd rather be in the room than on the outside. I'd want to be one of the people arguing about who owns the robots. Kofi would call that naive, and he might be right.

say: I'd say the gains **belong to everyone**, since they're built on our work.
I'd campaign for **shared income** or **public ownership** of robot fleets.
think: My run goes around **2031**, and the **control room** jobs go in 2028.
I'd be **thirty-one** with no driving or office job to step into.
do: Start training as a **wind turbine technician** in the first year.
Use **AI tools** to learn the new trade faster.
Keep my **savings** and index fund untouched.
feel: **Anxious**, but also **excited**, which feels wrong to admit.
S2.quote: If AI is going to beat me, it may as well teach me first.
fieldNote: She sees that the **fallback job** she planned disappears even earlier than her own.
Her **savings and skills** give her a sense of control, even in the fastest picture.
She is unusually **excited**, wanting a say in **who owns** the robots.

steps.text: Start a wind turbine technician course while still on nights
Use her AI assistant to study for the new trade
Campaign for public ownership of robot truck fleets
Sign up new union members at the parcel hub

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this fairly, so if it's not fair, that's politics, not technology. I'd be pushing the union to win a retraining fund from the parcel company now. And I'd tell everyone to learn the AI tools, because they're not going away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My driving goes around 2034, when I'm thirty-four. That's enough time to finish a whole trade and still be young. I think I'd actually come out of this one alright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving nights for two more years and save hard, maybe four hundred a month. Then I'd start a proper turbine or electrical apprenticeship in year three. Meanwhile I'd use the tools every day to get ready, quizzes, plans, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's manageable. More like planning a move than a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the hub in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect the planners to vanish around 2031, then the first robot trucks on the night motorway runs, maybe with a person sitting in for safety at first. I might even take a safety-driver shift, getting paid to watch the robot truck that's replacing me. Weird, but it would fund the apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kofi in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit him down at the services at two in the morning and tell him to start something now, not in 2033. He'd tell me to mind my own business. But I'd keep at it, and send him links.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to be fair, so unfairness is **politics**.
I'd push the union to win a **retraining fund** from the company now.
think: My driving goes around **2034**, enough time to finish **a whole trade**.
I'd likely come out of this one **alright**.
do: Drive nights for **two more years** and save about four hundred a month.
Start a **turbine or electrical apprenticeship** in year three.
Use **AI tools** daily to prepare for the change.
S3.quote: I might even take a safety-driver shift, getting paid to watch the robot truck that's replacing me.
fieldNote: Five years turns her plan into an **orderly sequence**: save, then apprentice.
She'd accept a **safety-driver** role with clear eyes about what it means.
She keeps **pressing a colleague** to act, even against his wishes.

steps.text: Save about four hundred a month from night-shift pay
Start a turbine or electrical apprenticeship in year three
Use AI quizzes daily to prepare for the apprenticeship
Push the union for a company-paid retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say this is a chance to do it properly, and I'd hold the government and the company to that. Online I'd be the annoying optimist. At work I'd be telling people this is the decade to learn something new on the company's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm fine. I'm thirty-nine in 2039, with years of driving money banked, and probably a second trade already. The thinking side changes in 2036, but I'm barely in the thinking side anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing nights for a few years and invest steadily. Around 2030, I'd start a trade, probably electrical, because robots and turbines all need wiring. I'd also keep running the union branch so the older drivers get a fair deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten years that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people waste it, like we wasted the warnings about lots of things. If the government sits on its hands till 2037, it's the same mess as the fast one, just later. That's what the union is for, keeping the pressure on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd invest steadily. In what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The same boring index fund, maybe a bit more each year. I've thought about buying shares in a robot truck company, and I hate that I've thought about it. It feels like betting on my own job going.

say: I'd say a **decade** is a chance to do it **properly**.
I'd tell coworkers to learn something new on the **company's time**.
think: I'm **fine**: thirty-nine in 2039, with savings and likely a **second trade**.
The **thinking side** changes in 2036, but I barely work in it.
do: Drive nights for a few years and **invest** steadily in the index fund.
Keep running the **union branch** for older drivers.
S4.quote: I've thought about buying shares in a robot truck company, and I hate that I've thought about it.
fieldNote: She sees **wasted time** as the real risk of the slow picture.
Her **mixed feelings** about owning robot-truck shares show her values pulling at her money sense.
With a decade, her mood settles into **real calm**.

steps.text: Add a bit more to her index fund each year
Start an electrical trade course around 2030
Keep running the union branch with a focus on older drivers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the job I'd move into goes even before mine does, and there's no time to finish a trade. What would help is a retraining income, so I could stop nights and study full time, and the union having a real say in how the robot fleets roll out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. Every robot truck saves someone a driver's wage, and that money goes somewhere. I'd want to know where before anyone tells me to be happy about it.

headlineQuote: Every robot truck saves someone a driver's wage, and that money goes somewhere.
portrait: Yara is a **27-year-old** night trunking driver for a parcel network, eight months on artics and still clumsy at **coupling**.
She uses **AI tools** daily and has nine months saved plus a small **index fund**.
She knows her **motorway run** is the most exposed driving job and plans to move into a hands-on trade.
She's an active **union** member who wants workers to share in the gains from robots.
She moves from **calm** to **anxious** in the fastest picture and back to calm with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her planned control room job vanishes before her driving does.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining income** so she could stop nights and study full time.
A real **union say** in how robot fleets are rolled out.
